title: Download buttons do not work inside iframes
body:
### Describe the bug

Download buttons on components do not work when the app is embedded in an iframe.
Try to use the download buttons on the output image of [this example](https://www.gradio.app/docs/examples) or the output video of [this example](https://www.gradio.app/docs/video).

The reason seems to be same as #6486 where `<a download="...">` does not work for different origins, while the embedded app has a different origin from the parent page.

Introducing the same trick as #6486 to all the download buttons would be one solution.

Written above.

title: [Data] ray.data.read_delta silently drops columns on Delta tables with column mapping enabled
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

`ray.data.read_delta` silently produces an incorrect schema when reading a Delta table that has **Delta Column Mapping** enabled. Columns added after column mapping was enabled are stored in the physical parquet files using UUID-based physical names (e.g. `col-4d014c4b-7d15-4d7b-a89e-blah-blah`). The Delta log contains the mapping from these UUIDs to logical column names, but `ray.data.read_delta` does not apply this translation. As a result, the returned dataset's schema contains UUID column names for those columns rather than their logical names, and any attempt to select or cast those columns by their logical name raises a `KeyError`.

## Root Cause Chain

1. `ray.data.read_delta` calls `DeltaTable(path, version=version).file_uris()` from `deltalake` to get parquet paths, then passes them to `ray.data.read_parquet`.
2. `ray.data.read_parquet` infers the dataset schema from `pq_ds.fragments[0].physical_schema` — the first parquet file's raw schema.
3. For a column-mapping-enabled Delta table, the physical parquet file stores columns using UUID names. The logical name translation lives in the Delta log metadata, which `deltalake 1.6.1` does not apply to the physical schema exposed to Ray.
4. The resulting dataset schema contains `col-4d014c4b-7d15-4d7b-a89e-<redacted>  double` where `<string column_name> double` is expected.

## Observed Schema (excerpt)

```
is_2_way                                       bool       ← last logical name
col-4d014c4b-7d15-4d7b-a89e-40dfdca76a22      double     ← should be a logical name
col-8c0bb653-f5db-4b02-a361-d29086e7f2ed      double
...
_row-id-col-9e9b0ae3-...                       int64
_row-commit-version-col-7bc4f86e-...           int64
```

- `DESCRIBE TABLE` confirms real column name exists at ordinal position 356 with type `double`
- `SHOW TBLPROPERTIES` confirms `delta.columnMapping.mode` is enabled on the table
- `DESCRIBE HISTORY` shows no `ADD COLUMN` operations — the column has existed since table creation; only its physical representation changed when column mapping was enabled
- Downgrading `deltalake` to `0.x` (which applied column mapping translation correctly) resolves the issue

## Expected Behavior

`ray.data.read_delta` should apply the Delta log's column mapping metadata to translate physical UUID column names to their logical names before constructing the dataset schema, consistent with how `deltalake 0.x` and Databricks' native readers behave.

## Further diagnostics

Per Anyscale's suggestion, we supplied a schema on read:

```python
dt = DeltaTable("s3://my-bucket/my-table",
                storage_options={"AWS_REGION": "...})

col_map = {
    field.metadata.get("delta.columnMapping.physicalName", field.name): field.name
    for field in dt.schema().fields
}

ds = ray.data.read_unity_catalog(...)
ds = ds.rename_columns(col_map)
```
This fixes reads (though ideally would not be required), but is incompatible with adding `row_filter`s to read_unity_catalog calls because row filters using logical table names are not mapped to the physical column name. The filter is then silently ignored, causing a full table scan.

Per Anyscale, it seems like we should've hit [this](https://github.com/delta-io/delta-rs/blob/main/python/deltalake/table.py#L1023) error from deltalake, but did not.

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: 2.55.1
- deltalake: 1.6.1
- PyArrow: 21.0.0
- Python: 3.11

### Reproduction script

Nontrivial to reproduce in isolation as this requires a databricks table with column mapping.

### Issue Severity

None

title: [core][adag] Throw unrecoverable actor exceptions to top-level `ray.get`
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Sometimes the actor execution loop will encounter an exception that it cannot recover from. For example, if a type hint is used to indicate that a tensor shape does not change, actors may exchange data through NCCL only. Then, if any exception occurs in a sender actor, the sender actor must exit because it will not be able to pass the exception to a downstream actor. Thus, in this case the entire DAG shuts down. The sender's stacktrace is printed to its stdout/stderr, but there is on programmatic way for the driver to retrieve the error.

Ideally, we would throw the root exception to the top-level refs returned by `dag.execute`. That way the user can catch the exception instead of only printing the stacktrace in the failing actor.

One tricky detail is identifying the root exception. Once one actor shuts down, it will close its sending/receiving channels, and the others will also fail with a `RayChannelError`. Also, more than one actor may fail. So ideally we should try to identify the earliest actor task in the DAG that failed.

title: [Data] Pipeline deadlocks when streaming generator tasks vanish from Ray Core without ending their stream
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Ray Data's streaming executor can deadlock when a Ray Core task disappears (e.g., worker crash during startup, task lost from scheduler) without the streaming generator's output stream being properly terminated via `MarkEndOfStream`.

**Expected**: The pipeline should detect that the underlying task is no longer running and either retry or propagate the error.

**Actual**: The pipeline hangs indefinitely. `process_completed_tasks` calls `ray.wait(timeout=0.1)` on the `ObjectRefGenerator`, which keeps returning "not ready" because the stream never received an end-of-stream marker. Meanwhile, `num_active_tasks() > 0` prevents `has_execution_finished()` from returning `True`, so the scheduling loop spins forever.

### Observed in production

A training job with a large Ray Data pipeline (71,428 blocks) got stuck at 71,420/71,428 blocks (8 blocks remaining from 2 tasks). Ray Data reported 2 active tasks, but Ray Core had no corresponding running tasks. The pipeline hung for over 2 hours with no progress until the job was manually aborted.

The cluster had a `.pth` file poisoning issue (binary PyTorch checkpoint files placed in `site-packages/` as `.pth` files) that caused new worker processes to crash during `init_import_site` with `UnicodeDecodeError`. This likely caused the 2 remaining tasks' workers to die during startup, before the streaming generator mechanism could properly clean up.

### Root cause

Ray Data relies solely on the streaming generator's `_next_sync()` raising `StopIteration` to detect task completion. This EOF signal is produced when Ray Core calls `MarkEndOfStream` on the stream, which happens in:
- `MarkTaskReturnObjectsFailed` → `MarkEndOfStream(generator_id, -1)` on task failure
- `CompletePendingTask` → `MarkEndOfStream(generator_id, num_returns)` on normal completion
- `MarkTaskCanceled` → `MarkEndOfStream(generator_id, -1)` on cancellation

If any of these paths are skipped (e.g., the task was never properly registered, or the failure propagation path has a gap), the stream never ends and Ray Data hangs.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray nightly (master branch)

### Reproduction script

The issue is difficult to reproduce deterministically as it depends on the specific failure mode of the worker process. It was observed in a production environment with 8 GPU workers and 8 CPU data nodes running a large-scale training pipeline.

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

body: ### What happened + What you expected to happen I encountered a significant memory leak in the Python 3.14 build, which did not occur in the Python 3.13 build. I am using Python 3.14.5, this minor version removes the incremental garbage collector (gc) and reverts to the Python 3.13 gc behaviour, so this memory leak is not related to garbage collection. I think there are some incompatibilities between the `boost` library underneath Ray Core and Python 3.14, perhaps related to https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/139653 ? While running Ray Tune with PyTorch Lightning, CUDA throws a GPU out-of-memory error after several trial scheduler terminations. Removal of the scheduler alleviates the issue. It has been reproduce with both ASHA and Median Stopping Rule.
Using HyperOpt for tuning.

### Versions / Dependencies

Docker image: rayproject/ray:3341fa-py38-gpu
ray: 2.0.0.dev0
ray-lightning: 0.3.0
pytorch: 1.11.0
pytorch-lightning: 1.5.10
cudatoolkit: 11.3.1

### Reproduction script

```python

def tune_train(tune_config):

    ray.tune.utils.wait_for_gpu(target_util=0.05)

    # update config object
    for k,v in tune_config.items():
        try:

        setattr(config, k, v)

    # Instatiate dataset
    dataset = LitDataset(config=config)
    # Instatiate model
    lit_model = LitModule(config=config)
    # Get trial save dir
    trial_dir = ray.tune.get_trial_dir()
    # Callbacks/strategies

    callbacks = [TuneReportCallback(
                        metrics={"loss": "val_loss"}),

                        monitor='val_loss', dirpath=trial_dir,
                        filename='{epoch:02d}-{val_loss:.10f}',
                        save_top_k=config.SAVE_TOP_K,

    gpu_monitor = pl.callbacks.GPUStatsMonitor()
    callbacks.append(gpu_monitor)

    # Trainer

def run_tuning():

if __name__ == '__main__':

title: [Datasets] Actors are incorrectly cached in local mode
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

When running an operation on a dataset (such as map, or map_batches), and using an actor strategy by passing in a CallableClass as the `fn`, and `compute="actors"`, the first actor class that is used will be cached and re-used, even if subsequent calls specify a new actor class. This only seems to be the case when ray has been initialised with `local_mode=True`.

### Versions / Dependencies

ray==1.13.0
Python 3.8.13

### Reproduction script

```python
import ray

class Actor1:
    def __call__(self, item):
        return "a1"

class Actor2:
    def __call__(self, item):
        return "a2"

ray.init(num_cpus=1, local_mode=True)

data = ray.data.from_items(["a"]).map(Actor1, compute="actors").take_all(1)
assert data == ["a1"], f"expected ['a1'], not {data}"

data = ray.data.from_items(["a"]).map(Actor2, compute="actors").take_all(1)
assert data == ["a2"], f"expected ['a2'], not {data}"
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

title: [Serve] Recovering replicas: long-poll broadcast can empty routable replica set and briefly halt traffic
body:
### Problem

When the Serve controller recovers state after a restart (or similar), existing replica actors are re-registered in `RECOVERING` before they transition to `RUNNING`. The long-poll `DEPLOYMENT_TARGETS` update is built from “running” replica infos only (`RUNNING` / `PENDING_MIGRATION`), so it can broadcast an **empty or sharply reduced** replica list while replicas are still `RECOVERING`. Proxies and routers apply that snapshot and **temporarily route no traffic**, causing a short cluster-wide availability blip.

There is an existing TODO on this path in `DeploymentState.recover_current_state_from_replica_actor_names` noting that this **halts all traffic in the cluster briefly** and suggesting a **grace period** before broadcasting that update.

### Expected behavior

During recovery, traffic should **not** be dropped merely because replicas are not yet marked `RUNNING` in the controller, as long as the replica actors are still healthy and will imminently become routable again.

### Likely root cause

- `get_running_replica_infos()` excludes `RECOVERING`, so `broadcast_running_replicas_if_changed()` can advertise no backends while recovery is in progress.
- `done_recovering_event` is also set after `RECOVERING_LONG_POLL_BROADCAST_TIMEOUT_S` (default 10s) to unblock long poll, which can align with broadcasts **while replicas are still recovering**.

### Suggested direction

Introduce a **grace period or gating** so the first post-recovery `DEPLOYMENT_TARGETS` broadcast does not replace a healthy routable set with an empty one solely due to `RECOVERING` state—or defer long-poll notifications until replicas have transitioned or a safer snapshot is available. Revisit the interaction between `done_recovering_event`, `RECOVERING_LONG_POLL_BROADCAST_TIMEOUT_S`, and `DeploymentStateManager.update()` STEP 7 (broadcast).

title: [Jobs] JobInfoStorageClient.put_status uses assert for state machine protection, ineffective under python -O
body:
### Describe the bug

`JobInfoStorageClient.put_status` uses `assert False` to prevent invalid job status transitions (e.g., SUCCEEDED → FAILED). However, `assert` statements are removed when Python runs with the `-O` flag, silently disabling the state machine protection.

### How to reproduce

```bash
# Under python -O, assert statements are removed:
python -O -c "
import sys
print(f'optimize={sys.flags.optimize}')  # optimize=1
# The assert on common.py is compiled away.
# Invalid transitions like SUCCEEDED -> FAILED are no longer blocked.
"
```

Without `-O` (normal mode), `assert False` raises `AssertionError` and blocks the invalid transition.

With `-O`, the assertion is silently skipped and the transition is allowed.

### Expected behavior

Invalid status transitions should always be rejected, regardless of Python optimization level.

### Actual behavior

Under `python -O`, the assertion is removed by the compiler. Invalid transitions like `SUCCEEDED → FAILED` and `FAILED → RUNNING` are silently allowed, corrupting the job state machine.

### Root cause

In `python/ray/dashboard/modules/job/common.py`:

```python
if status != old_info.status and old_info.status.is_terminal():
    assert False, "Attempted to change job status from a terminal state."
```

`assert` is a debugging tool, not a control flow mechanism. Python's `-O` flag removes all assert statements at compile time.

### Possible fix

Replace `assert False` with `raise RuntimeError(...)` to ensure the check is always active:

```python
if status != old_info.status and old_info.status.is_terminal():
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"Attempted to change job status from a terminal state: "
        f"{old_info.status} -> {status}"
    )
```

### Environment

- Ray version: master branch (commit `HEAD`)
- Python version: 3.12

title: [Core] Cheap object-size lookup API for budget-aware batched ray.get in Ray Data
body:
## Description

Expose a cheap, no-RPC API to look up the byte size of one or more `ObjectRef`s **without fetching the object data**. Ray Core already tracks `data + metadata size` per object in the owner's directory (it's used internally for OOM / spill / scheduling decisions); we just don't have a stable Python API to read it for refs whose data hasn't been pulled to the local node yet.

Concretely, propose one of:

1. **Document + extend the existing `ray.experimental.get_local_object_locations`** so its `object_size` field is reliably populated for refs whose owning task has yielded but whose data hasn't been transferred to the local node (the streaming-generator case below). The function exists; the question is whether `object_size` is `None` or a real integer in that specific state. If it's currently `None`, the fix is to also expose the owner-side size (which Ray Core knows from `SealOwnedObject`) rather than only the in-store size.

2. **(Lighter alternative)** A focused `ray.experimental.get_object_sizes(refs) -> List[Optional[int]]` that is exactly that — sugar over the existing locations call, returning only the sizes. Simpler call signature for the by-far most common use case.

No new RPCs and no new state — this is purely a Python entry point onto data Ray Core already maintains.

## Use case

This is motivated by the Ray Data scheduler's per-iteration batched `ray.get` of block metadata in PR [#63483](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/63483) (\"[Data] Batch ray.get of block metadata in process_completed_tasks\").

### Today's flow

The StreamingExecutor scheduling thread pulls completed-task outputs from per-task `ObjectRefGenerator`s. Each yield produces a pair `(block_ref, meta_ref)`. The metadata blob (a pickled `BlockMetadataWithSchema`) carries `meta.size_bytes` — the **block's** byte size — which is the unit the downstream backpressure budget (`max_bytes_to_read`) is denominated in.

The new batched path in [#63483](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/63483) does:

```
for task in ready_tasks:
    while task.peek_pending_pair() is not None: pass      # drain gen
refs = ⋃ task.uncached_pending_meta_refs() for task in ready_tasks
bytes_list = ray.get(refs, timeout=METADATA_GET_TIMEOUT_S)  # ONE round-trip
for task: task.cache_prefetched_meta_bytes({ref: bytes, ...})
for task: task.on_data_ready(remaining_output_budget[op])  # emit RefBundles
```

### The chicken-and-egg

The downstream-emit budget is in `meta.size_bytes`. `meta.size_bytes` lives **inside** the metadata blob. So to know whether a pair's block fits the budget, we have to fetch its metadata first. The batched `ray.get` is therefore necessarily speculative — it fetches metadata for every immediately-ready pair across every ready task, even pairs whose blocks won't actually be emitted this iteration (because budget runs out or the op is backpressured mid-batch).

Per-iteration over-fetch ceiling changed accordingly:

| | over-fetch ceiling |
|---|---|
| pre-PR (per-pair `ray.get`) | at most 1 pair past budget |
| post-PR (batched) | up to the union of every ready task's gen backlog |

The bytes survive across iterations (`_cached_meta_bytes` is keyed by `meta_ref` on the task), so it's not wasted work — the next iteration consumes from cache without a new `ray.get`. But it does inflate the per-iteration metadata fetch volume and amplifies the straggler effect (one slow ref blocks the whole batched call).

### What `object_size` would unlock

The block's byte size (the actual budget unit) **is already known to Ray Core** the moment the worker seals the block — well before the driver issues `ray.get` on the metadata. If we can read it cheaply, the scheduler does:

```python
# in process_completed_tasks, after the peek loop
new_pairs = [...]                                          # (block_ref, meta_ref) tuples just peeked
block_refs = [bref for bref, _ in new_pairs]
sizes = ray.experimental.get_object_sizes(block_refs)      # cheap, local, no RPC

cum = 0
to_fetch = []
for (bref, mref), size in zip(new_pairs, sizes):
    if size is None or cum + size > remaining_budget:
        break          # leave the rest queued for next iter (uncached)
    cum += size
    to_fetch.append(mref)

# Bulk ray.get only the meta_refs whose blocks fit the budget.
bytes_list = ray.get(to_fetch, timeout=METADATA_GET_TIMEOUT_S)
```

This turns the bulk `ray.get` into a **budget-aware** fetch:

- Metadata is fetched only for pairs whose blocks will be emitted this iteration.
- Per-iteration over-fetch ceiling drops back to ~1 pair past budget (the prefix sum can overshoot by one before the loop breaks).
- Straggler amplification shrinks: smaller, more predictable batch sizes.
- The `_cached_meta_bytes` carryover across iterations becomes redundant — the cleaner design fetches exactly what it'll consume.

### Why this isn't fixable purely in Ray Data

We considered several Ray-Data-internal mitigations:

- **Hard cap on batch size** (`MAX_REFS_PER_BATCH=256`) — bounds the blast radius but doesn't make the fetch budget-aware.
- **Estimate size from prior `_last_block_meta`** — works for steady-state uniform blocks, fails when block sizes vary (which is common after filtering / map operators that change cardinality).
- **Change the streaming generator protocol** to yield `(block_ref, size_int, meta_ref)` triples so size arrives inline — biggest API surface change, requires every Ray-Data task generator to comply.

A simple Ray Core size accessor is by far the smallest, most reusable change. Anything else that batches refs and wants to respect a byte budget (e.g., shuffle, custom collectives, distributed accumulators) needs the same primitive.

## Sketch of the API

Two flavors, increasing in scope. Either works for the Ray Data case.

**(a) Investigation + docs first:** clarify in `ray.experimental.get_local_object_locations` whether `object_size` is `None` for not-yet-locally-resident refs whose owner knows the size, and if so, populate it from the owner's directory entry. No new symbol.

**(b) New focused symbol:**

```python
def ray.experimental.get_object_sizes(
    refs: List[ObjectRef],
) -> List[Optional[int]]:
    \"\"\"Return the byte size of each object as known to Ray Core, without
    fetching the object data. Returns None for any ref whose size is not
    yet known (e.g., the producing task has not yet sealed the object).

    Cheap, no RPCs — reads from the local core worker's owner directory
    (for refs we own) or the in-store metadata (for refs whose data is
    local).
    \"\"\"
```

Implementation note: behind the binding, this should be the same code path that `CObjectLocation::GetObjectSize()` already exercises in `_raylet.pyx:507`; the question is just whether the owner side already publishes the size before the local store has the data.

## Alternatives considered

- **Iterative bounded batches**: fetch K refs at a time, consume, fetch K more if budget remains. Defeats the per-iteration round-trip win that PR #63483 exists to deliver.
- **Conservative size estimate** (running average of prior `meta.size_bytes`): works in steady state, but Ray Data's block sizes vary substantially across stages (Read → Map → Filter all produce different distributions).
- **Async / streaming `ray.get`** (`on_ready` callback per ref): helps the straggler half of the problem, doesn't help the budget half.

## Out of scope

- Whether the budget logic itself should change (it shouldn't — it's correct as-is, the issue is purely \"what to fetch in the first place\").
- Cross-task `ray.get` batching strategy itself; that's settled in [#63483](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/63483).
- The other 5000-task scaling issue (`update_usages` / `safe_round` dominating dispatch). Separate follow-up.

---

cc Ray Data / Ray Core teams. Happy to prototype both the binding and the Ray Data side once the right shape is settled.
label: actionable

title: # [Bug] Ray serve replica creates circular exception chain for non-grpc requests
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

After upgrading from Ray 2.53 to 2.54, replicas freeze whenever user code raises an unhandled exception. The controller kills them via health checks, new ones spin up, and the cycle repeats. Traced it to a circular `__cause__` chain on the exception object.

In `handle_request_with_rejection` (and the other two handle methods), there's this pattern:

```python
except Exception as e:
    raise self._maybe_wrap_grpc_exception(e, request_metadata) from e
```

For non-gRPC requests (called via `DeploymentHandle`), [`_maybe_wrap_grpc_exception`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.54.0/python/ray/serve/_private/replica.py#L1308-L1325) returns `e` unchanged (L1325: `return e`), so this effectively becomes `raise e from e` --> Python sets `e.__cause__ = e`.

**Impact**: Error-reporting tools (like Sentry, Bugsnag, etc) that walks `__cause__` chains without cycle detection will spin forever. That blocks the replica's main thread, starves health checks, and the controller kills the replica.

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: 2.54.0
- Python: 3.11
- OS: Linux x86_64


### Reproduction script

```python
import asyncio, logging, ray
from ray import serve

class CauseWalker(logging.Handler):
    """Walks __cause__ chain — standard for error-reporting tools."""
    def emit(self, record):
        if record.exc_info and record.exc_info[1]:
            exc = record.exc_info[1]
            while exc.__cause__:  # infinite loop when __cause__ is self
                exc = exc.__cause__

@serve.deployment(health_check_period_s=2, health_check_timeout_s=2)
class App:
    def __init__(self):
        logging.getLogger("ray.serve").addHandler(CauseWalker())

    async def fail(self):
        raise ValueError("user code exception")


async def main():
    ray.init()
    handle = serve.run(App.bind(), name="repro")
    try:
        await handle.fail.remote()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Caller got: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    await asyncio.sleep(15)  # wait for health check failures
    serve.shutdown()
    ray.shutdown()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

Current output: The replica hangs after the exception and the controller kills it:
```
WARNING -- Didn't receive health check response for replica ... after 2.0s, marking it unhealthy.
WARNING -- Replica ... failed the health check 3 times in a row, marking it unhealthy.
WARNING -- Replica ... failed health check, stopping it.
```

**Expected output**: The error reporting handler reports the bug and the replica continues processing other requests.

**Suggested fix:** Only use `from e` when the exception is actually wrapped:

```python
except Exception as e:
    wrapped = self._maybe_wrap_grpc_exception(e, request_metadata)
    if wrapped is not e:
        raise wrapped from e
    raise
```
I can raise a quick PR if required.

### Issue Severity

High: It blocks me from completing my task.
label: actionable

title: [Core] AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'trace' in 2.54.0
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

 Ray Bug Report: _opentelemetry Serialization Asymmetry in Ray Client Mode (2.54.0+)                                                              
                                                                                                                                                   
  Component: ray/util/tracing/tracing_helper.py, ray/_private/function_manager.py, ray/actor.py                                                    
                                                                                                                                                   
  Versions affected: 2.54.0, 2.55.1 (and likely all subsequent)                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                   
  Regression from: 2.53.0                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                   
  ---                                                                                                                                              
  Summary                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                                                   
  When using Ray Client (ray.init("ray://...")) with the --tracing-startup-hook flag configured on the head node, actor __init__ crashes on the    
  worker with:                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                   
  AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'trace'                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                   
  inside _resume_span in tracing_helper.py.                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                   
  ---                                                                                                                                              
  Root cause                                                                                                                                       

  Ray 2.54.0 made two related changes:

  1. function_manager.py now calls _inject_tracing_into_class(actor_class) on the worker side after loading the actor class from GCS.
  2. tracing_helper.py added a __ray_tracing_wrapped__ marker so that worker-side re-injection skips already-wrapped methods (to prevent
  double-wrapping after the cloudpickle round-trip).

  Together these create a serialization asymmetry when the driver is a Ray Client (not a full cluster node):

  - On the driver, _make_actor calls _inject_tracing_into_class, which wraps actor methods with _resume_span closures and stamps them
  __ray_tracing_wrapped__ = True.
  - The _resume_span closure captures two module-level names from tracing_helper:
    - _is_tracing_enabled — a function reference. cloudpickle serializes top-level functions by module reference, so on the worker it resolves to
  the worker's live function, which returns True (the worker called _enable_tracing() via the startup hook).
    - _opentelemetry — a variable value. cloudpickle serializes this by value at pickle time. On a Ray Client driver, _enable_tracing() is never
  called, so this value is None.
  - On the worker, _inject_tracing_into_class sees __ray_tracing_wrapped__ = True and skips re-wrapping. The stale closure is used as-is.
  - When __init__ runs, _resume_span evaluates _is_tracing_enabled() → True and _ray_trace_ctx is non-None (injected by _tracing_actor_creation on
  the driver because the cluster has tracing enabled), so it proceeds to call _opentelemetry.trace → None.trace → crash.

  In Ray 2.53.0 neither of these changes existed: function_manager.py did not call _inject_tracing_into_class on the worker, and there was no
  __ray_tracing_wrapped__ guard, so the worker always re-wrapped with a fresh closure containing its own valid _opentelemetry.

  ---
  What does NOT fix it

  Upgrading opentelemetry-instrumentation-grpc: The worker pod logs show circular import errors from this package during startup, which look
  suspicious. These are a red herring — they are a nuisance from gRPC initialization order but do not affect _opentelemetry being None.

  Calling _enable_tracing() on the driver after ray.init(): This sets _global_is_tracing_enabled = True on the driver, which activates
  _invocation_actor_class_remote_span (the wrapper around ActorClass.remote()). That wrapper does:

  span.set_attribute("ray.actor_id", result._ray_actor_id.hex())

  In Ray Client mode, result is a ClientActorRef, which has no _ray_actor_id attribute — a second, different crash. So _enable_tracing() cannot be
  called on a Ray Client driver.

  ---
  Workaround

  After ray.init("ray://...") succeeds on the driver, populate _opentelemetry directly without setting _global_is_tracing_enabled:

  import ray.util.tracing.tracing_helper as _th
  if _th._opentelemetry is None:
      _th._opentelemetry = _th._OpenTelemetryProxy()

  This ensures the pickled _resume_span closure carries a valid proxy instead of None, while leaving tracing disabled on the driver so
  _invocation_actor_class_remote_span remains a no-op.

  ---
  Proper fix suggestion

  _inject_tracing_into_class should not serialize _opentelemetry by value into the closure. Instead, _resume_span should always read _opentelemetry
   from the module at call time (i.e., reference the module, not close over the variable). Alternatively, _invocation_actor_class_remote_span
  should guard against ClientActorRef before accessing _ray_actor_id, which would make calling _enable_tracing() on a Ray Client driver safe.


### Versions / Dependencies

ray 2.54.0 (happens in latest version as well), doesn't happen in ray 2.53.0
python 3.12
os ubuntu 22.04

### Reproduction script

 ray_real_reproducer.py
------

"""
Ray 2.54.0 bug: AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'trace'
when using Ray Client (ray://) + --tracing-startup-hook.

Root cause: cloudpickle snapshots the actor class __globals__ dict by value.
_opentelemetry=None on the Ray Client driver is baked in. The
__ray_tracing_wrapped__ guard (new in 2.54.0) prevents re-injection on the
worker, so the frozen None survives. Worker's _enable_tracing() never reaches
the deserialized function's frozen globals. Crash follows in _resume_span.

Fix: after ray.init("ray://..."), set th._opentelemetry directly. Do NOT call
_enable_tracing() — it also sets _global_is_tracing_enabled=True which
activates _invocation_actor_class_remote_span on the driver, which calls
result._ray_actor_id.hex() — crashes on ClientActorRef (no _ray_actor_id).

Requires: ray==2.54.0, ray_tracing_hook.py on PYTHONPATH.

Start Ray head before running this script:
  ray start --head --ray-client-server-port=20001 \\
    --tracing-startup-hook=ray_tracing_hook:setup

Then run:
  python ray_real_reproducer.py          # shows the bug
  python ray_real_reproducer.py --fix    # shows the fix
"""
import sys, ray
import ray.util.tracing.tracing_helper as th

ray.init("ray://localhost:20001"

title: [Data] read_parquet() fails with ArrowNotImplementedError on Parquet files with nested column types
body:
### What happened + What you expected to happen
ray.data.read_parquet() fails with ArrowNotImplementedError: Nested data conversions not implemented for chunked array outputs when reading Parquet files containing nested column types (list<struct>, map, struct with nested fields).

The error occurs in the ReadParquet operator before any user code executes. The expectation is that read_parquet() should be able to read Parquet files with nested types without error.

  **Stack Trace**

  ray.exceptions.RayTaskError(ArrowNotImplementedError): ray::ReadParquet() (pid=2617, ip=10.150.213.97)
    File "ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/map_transformer.py", line 102, in call
      for b_out in map_transformer.apply_transform(iter(blocks), ctx):
    File "ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/map_transformer.py", line 84, in shapeblocks
      yield from self._post_process(results)
    File "ray/data/_internal/execution/operators/map_transformer.py", line 412, in applytransform
      for result in results:
    File "ray/data/_internal/planner/plan_read_op.py", line 107, in do_read
      yield from read_task()
    File "ray/data/datasource/datasource.py", line 218, in call
      yield from result
    File "ray/data/_internal/datasource/parquet_datasource.py", line 472, in read_fragments
      for table in iterate_with_retry(
    File "ray/data/_internal/util.py", line 1434, in iterate_with_retry
      raise e from None
    File "ray/data/_internal/util.py", line 1415, in iterate_with_retry
      for item_index, item in enumerate(iterable):
    File "ray/data/_internal/datasource/parquet_datasource.py", line 527, in read_batches_from
      for batch in fragment.to_batches(
    File "pyarrow/_dataset.pyx", line 3934, in _iterator
    File "pyarrow/_dataset.pyx", line 3524, in pyarrow._dataset.TaggedRecordBatchIterator.__next__
    File "pyarrow/error.pxi", line 155, in pyarrow.lib.pyarrow_internal_check_status
    File "pyarrow/error.pxi", line 92, in pyarrow.lib.check_status
    pyarrow.lib.ArrowNotImplementedError: Nested data conversions not implemented for chunked array outputs




**Likely Root Cause**

  upstream PyArrow limitation:
  - https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/ARROW-5030
  - https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/21526
  - https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/32723

When Parquet row groups contain nested columns whose binary/string data exceeds PyArrow's internal chunking threshold (~2GB), the binary array builder splits the data into chunks. The nested array reconstruction code (WrapIntoListArray) cannot handle chunked arrays, raising ArrowNotImplementedError.

### Reproduction script

```
import os
import random
import string
import tempfile

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
import ray


def random_string(length: int) -> str:
    return "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_letters + string.digits, k=length))


def create_parquet_with_nested_columns(output_dir: str) -> str:
    os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

    # To trigger ARROW-5030, nested column data in a single row group must exceed ~2GB.
    # 2500 rows * 10 items/row * 100KB/item = ~2.5GB of nested string data.
    num_rows = 2500
    items_per_row = 10
    payload_size = 100_000  # 100KB per list item

    print(f"Generating {num_rows} rows with ~{items_per_row * payload_size / 1024 / 1024:.1f}MB "
          f"nested data per row (total ~{num_rows * items_per_row * payload_size / 1024 / 1024 / 1024:.1f}GB)...")

    ids = list(range(num_rows))

    # list<struct> column with large string payloads per item
    nested_data = [
        [
            {
                "key": f"item_{i}_{j}",
                "payload": random_string(payload_size),
                "value": random.randint(0, 10000),
            }
            for j in range(items_per_row)
        ]
        for i in ids
    ]

    schema = pa.schema([
        ("id", pa.int64()),
        ("nested_col", pa.list_(pa.struct([
            ("key", pa.string()),
            ("payload", pa.string()),
            ("value", pa.int64()),
        ]))),
    ])

    table = pa.table(
        {"id": ids, "nested_col": nested_data},
        schema=schema,
    )

    file_path = os.path.join(output_dir, "data.parquet")
    # Single large row group — all rows in one group to exceed the 2GB threshold
    pq.write_table(table, file_path, row_group_size=num_rows, use_dictionary=False)
    print(f"Wrote {file_path} ({os.path.getsize(file_path) / 1024 / 1024:.0f}MB on disk)")
    return output_dir


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"Ray: {ray.__version__}, PyArrow: {pa.__version__}")

    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="repro_nested_") as tmpdir:
        data_dir = create_parquet_with_nested_columns(tmpdir)

        ray.init()

        # This should fail with:
        #   ArrowNotImplementedError: Nested data conversions not implemented
        #   for chunked array outputs
        print("\nReading with ray.data.read_parquet()...")
        try:
            ds = ray.data.read_parquet(data_dir)
            for batch in ds.iter_batches(batch_format="pyarrow", batch_size=100):
                pass
            print("No error — bug did not reproduce (may need larger data or different PyArrow version)")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"ERROR: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
```



### Versions / Dependencies

Ray: 2.50.0
PyArrow: 19.0.1
Python: 3.9

### Issue Severity

None

### Description                                                                                                                    
Models with `trust_remote_code=True` (e.g. MiniMax-M2.1) bundle custom Python config files. In `sglang_engine_proc.py`, the telemetry call:

```
hf_config = transformers.AutoConfig.from_pretrained(config.model_source)

The vLLM processor already handles all three. ray-project/ray#60344 further improves the vLLM path's download mode selection but does not address SGLang.


### Completion Criteria                                             
- Call `download_model_files()` before `AutoConfig.from_pretrained()`, using `EXCLUDE_SAFETENSORS` mode when `trust_remote_code=True` and `TOKENIZER_ONLY` otherwise
- Pass `trust_remote_code` from `config.engine_kwargs` to `AutoConfig.from_pretrained()`                                         
- Wrap in `try/except` so telemetry failures fall back to `DEFAULT_MODEL_ARCHITECTURE` instead of crashing

title: [Data] from_daft() PyArrow version check is obsolete, blocks all modern Daft installations
body:
## Problem

`ray.data.from_daft()` raises `RuntimeError` when PyArrow >= 14.0.0:

```python
# read_api.py line 3256
if pyarrow_version >= parse_version("14.0.0"):
    raise RuntimeError("`from_daft` only works with PyArrow 13 or lower.")
```

This check was added because Daft previously had compatibility issues with PyArrow >= 14 (see #53278). However, **Daft has since fixed this** — as of March 2026, Daft's minimum PyArrow requirement is >= 15.0.0.

## Impact

Any user with a modern Daft installation (which requires PyArrow >= 15) will hit this error and **cannot use `from_daft()` at all**. The previous advice to "just upgrade pyarrow" (#53278) is now inverted — users cannot downgrade PyArrow below 14 without also breaking Daft.

## Proposed Fix

1. Remove the PyArrow version check and `RuntimeError` from `from_daft()`
2. Remove the unused `get_pyarrow_version` and `parse_version` imports from `read_api.py`
3. Remove the `test_from_daft_raises_error_on_pyarrow_14` test
4. Remove the `@pytest.mark.skipif` from `test_daft_round_trip`

The function body simply calls `df.to_ray_dataset()`, which works fine with modern Daft + PyArrow combinations.

## References

- #53278 — original issue (closed as won't fix)
label: actionable

title: [Data] Remove obsolete PyArrow 9.0 version checks
body:
## What is the problem?

Ray Data contains obsolete version checks for PyArrow's object extension type feature, which was introduced in PyArrow 9.0.0. Since Ray's minimum required PyArrow version is already >= `9.0.0` (as specified in `python/requirements.txt`), these version checks are redundant and add unnecessary code complexity.

### Current code issues:

1. `MIN_PYARROW_VERSION_SCALAR_SUBCLASS` constant and `_object_extension_type_allowed()` function still exist but always return `True`
2. Conditional logic in `tensor_extensions/arrow.py` checks both version and config, making the code harder to understand
3. Tests are skipped based on version checks that will never fail

title: [Serve] Shutdown deletes KV checkpoints before teardown completes; can orphan replica actors
body:
### Problem

During Serve shutdown, application and deployment managers **delete their GCS KV checkpoints immediately** after initiating deletes (`ApplicationStateManager.shutdown`, `DeploymentStateManager.shutdown`), without waiting for graceful replica shutdown and in-memory state removal to finish. Checkpoint writes are also disabled while `_shutting_down` is set.

If the controller **crashes or is killed** after checkpoints are removed but **before** replicas finish stopping and deployment/application entries are fully removed, the cluster **loses the authoritative list of deployments/replicas** while **replica actors may still be running**, leading to **orphaned actors** and leaked resources.

### Expected behavior

Durable state should remain recoverable (or a clear shutdown-in-progress record should exist) **until** all shutdown goals are met—at minimum until replica actors intended for teardown are actually gone or explicitly tracked for cleanup.

title: BUG: `DataFrame.eval` inconsistently handles duplicated columns
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {'a': range(3), 'b': range(10, 13), 'c': range(3)}
).rename(columns={'b': 'a'})

print(df)
print(df.eval('a == 1'))
print(pd.eval('a == 1', resolvers=(df,)))
```

### Issue Description

`Dataframe.eval ` behaves differently from `pandas.eval()` when a `DataFrame` contains duplicated column names.

In the example above, the `DataFrame` has two columns named `a`. Evaluating the expression `a == 1` appears to only evaluate one of the duplicated columns (the second one in this case), and returning a `pandas.Series`

In contrast, `pd.eval( ... )` evaluates both duplicated columns and returns a `DataFrame`. 

Similar to #59950

### Expected Behavior

It would be helpful to clarify whether duplicated column names are intended to be supported in both APIs. 

Possible expected behaviors could include: 
* both methods behaving similarly
* raising an explicit exception when expressions reference duplicated names

### Location of the documentation

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/doc/source/development/contributing.rst

### Documentation problem

There is a typo/redundancy in these lines of code describing how to create a fork
```
git fetch upstream
get fetch upstream --tags
```

1. The first part of the issue is that the last line has a typo (`get` instead of `git`, and I can confirm the command failed when I tried to run it). Fixing the typo on the second line one would get
```
git fetch upstream
git fetch upstream --tags`
```
2. The second part of the issue is that when the typo is fixed, the first line becomes redundant, since the second line fetches everything the first one fetches and also fetches the tags.

### Suggested fix for documentation

One can replace the two lines above with a single one without typos and achieve the same result
```
git fetch upstream --tags`
```

**This is not sufficient.**

The issue appears in multiple places across the documentation (e.g., parameter descriptions and examples where {{ }} is rendered instead of { }). Just in `reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html` ([link](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html)), there are at least:

Just in `reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html` ([link](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html)), there are at least:

- The `date_format` example also uses double braces:  
  `date_format={{"col 2": "%d/%m/%Y", "col 3": "%a %d %b %Y"}}`.

- Parameter type description for `dtype` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{Hashable dtype}}`.

- Parameter type description for `converters` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{HashableCallable}}`.

- Parameter type description for `na_values` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{HashableIterable}}`.

- Enum values for `engine` render incorrectly as:  
  `engine {{‘c’, ‘python’, ‘pyarrow’}}`.

- Enum values for `quoting` render incorrectly as:  
  `{{0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL, ...}}`.

- Header renaming description renders placeholders incorrectly as:  
  `".{{count}}"`.

- Placeholder examples for unnamed columns render incorrectly as:  
  `"Unnamed: {{i}}"` and `"Unnamed: {{i}}_level_{{level}}"`.

- Several dictionary examples throughout the page use `{{ }}` instead of `{ }`, which makes the shown Python code invalid.

### Suggested fix for documentation

I assume the double braces were originally used to escape literal `{}` in docstrings that passed through a .format()/Substitution step. Since the formatting step is seemingly no longer applied (TBC?) in the current doc build, the escapes now leak into the rendered docs, so they should be replaced across the repo with normal braces only if we can confirm they're no longer necessary or we need to fix the build step.

import time

import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa


def bench(storage: str, rows: int = 1000, cols: int = 20) -> float:

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

ONE_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Budapest")
OTHER_TZ = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01 15:13:44.01234567", tz="Europe/Moscow")

# Example (works): different timezones, no NaT
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, OTHER_TZ]})
df1.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (works): same timezone, with NaT
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[ONE_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df2.max(axis=1) # Works

# Example (fails): different timezone, with NaT
df3 = pd.DataFrame({"time1":[ONE_TZ, ONE_TZ], "time2":[OTHER_TZ, pd.Timestamp("")]})
df3.max(axis=1) # Fails, as soon as we have a NaT
```

### Issue Description

In dataframes with datetime64 columns, max() fails with a `TypeError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timestamp' and 'float'` when 2 different timezones and NaT values are both present. As long as we have 1 timezone or no NaTs, everything works as expected. The default behavior of max() is skipping nans, and NaT is interpreted as such correctly with the same timezone. Once the timezone is different, it is treated as a float and the comparison fails.

It seems like during the max() operation, since timezones differ, rows are coerced into an `object` dtype. The NaT is leaking into the underlying numpy amax as a float instead of being safely skipped or masked out before the comparison occurs.

### Expected Behavior

Truly skipping NaTs as a default in max() before attempting the comparison of the remaining datetime64 values.

title: BUG: Plotting with duplicate column names gives misleading error
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
df.columns = ["a", "a"]

df.plot.hist()
# TypeError: no numeric data to plot

df.plot.box()
# TypeError: no numeric data to plot
```

### Issue Description

Plotting a DataFrame with duplicate column names raises `TypeError: no numeric data to plot`, even when all columns are numeric.

The root cause is in `MPLPlot.__init__` ([core.py line 193-195](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/core.py#L193-L195)):

```python
self.columns = [
    col for col in data.columns if is_numeric_dtype(data[col])
]
```

When columns are non-unique, `data[col]` returns a DataFrame instead of a Series. `is_numeric_dtype` returns `False` for DataFrames, so all duplicate-named columns are silently dropped, leaving `self.columns` empty.

Even if this filter were fixed (e.g. using positional indexing), duplicate column names would still break downstream in multiple places:

- `_ensure_frame` (line ~681): `data.loc[:, cols]` with duplicate names causes column expansion
- `_get_nseries` (line ~507): `len(self.columns)` double-counts duplicate names
- `_compute_plot_data` (line ~691): passes duplicate labels into `reconstruct_data_with_by` → `MultiIndex.from_product`, multiplying the problem
- Scatter/hexbin plots (lines ~1352, 1395): `data[x]`/`data[y]` return DataFrames instead of Series, breaking shape expectations

The plotting pipeline fundamentally relies on label-based indexing (`data[col]`, `data.loc[:, cols]`) at every stage, so duplicate columns can't work without significant rework.

### Expected Behavior

Either:
1. Raise a clear error early (e.g. `ValueError: plotting requires unique column names`), or
2. Handle duplicate columns correctly throughout the pipeline

Option 1 seems most practical given how pervasive the label-based indexing is.

title: BUG: HDFStore.select(where=...) silently returns empty DataFrame with datetime64[us] index
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import tempfile, os

print(f"pandas: {pd.__version__}")

idx = pd.date_range("2019-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="h")
print(f"Index dtype: {idx.dtype}")  # datetime64[us] in pandas 3.0

df = pd.DataFrame({"value": np.random.randn(len(idx))}, index=idx)
tmpfile = tempfile.mktemp(suffix=".h5")

df.to_hdf(tmpfile, key="test", mode="w", format="table")

with pd.HDFStore(tmpfile, mode="r") as store:
    # where query returns 0 rows (BUG)
    result = store.select("test", where="'index' >= '2020-01-01' & 'index' <= '2023-01-01'")
    print(f"With where: {len(result)} rows")  # 0 — wrong!

    # Without where + manual filter works fine
    all_data = store.select("test")
    filtered = all_data[(all_data.index >= "2020-01-01") & (all_data.index <= "2023-01-01")]
    print(f"Manual filter: {len(filtered)} rows")  # ~26305 — correct

os.unlink(tmpfile)
```

**Output (pandas 3.0.1):**

```
pandas: 3.0.1
Index dtype: datetime64[us]
With where: 0 rows
Manual filter: 26305 rows
```


### Issue Description

#### Summary
`HDFStore.select()` with string-based `where` conditions on a datetime index silently returns an empty DataFrame when the index has microsecond resolution (`datetime64[us]`). This is a regression in pandas 3.0, where the default datetime resolution changed from nanoseconds to microseconds.

#### Root cause
The stored index values are int64 microseconds (e.g. `1546300800000000` — 16 digits), but the `where` query engine appears to convert comparison dates to nanosecond int64 values (e.g. `1546300800000000000` — 19 digits). The mismatch means no rows ever match.

**Evidence:** forcing the index to nanosecond resolution before writing makes the query work:

```python
idx_ns = pd.date_range("2019-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="h").as_unit("ns")
df_ns = pd.DataFrame({"value": np.random.randn(len(idx_ns))}, index=idx_ns)
df_ns.to_hdf(tmpfile, key="test", mode="w", format="table")

with pd.HDFStore(tmpfile, mode="r") as store:
    result = store.select("test", where="'index' >= '2020-01-01' & 'index' <= '2023-01-01'")
    print(f"With where (ns): {len(result)} rows")  # 26305 — correct
```


### Expected Behavior

`store.select("test", where="'index' >= '2020-01-01'")` should return matching rows regardless of the datetime resolution of the stored index.

title: PERF: cache BlockManager.get_dtypes() result
body:
### Problem

`BaseBlockManager.get_dtypes()` (`pandas/core/internals/managers.py:339`) rebuilds an object array on every call:

```python
def get_dtypes(self) -> npt.NDArray[np.object_]:
    dtypes = np.array([blk.dtype for blk in self.blocks], dtype=object)
    return dtypes.take(self.blknos)
```

It's called from a number of hot paths — `df.dtypes`, `DataFrame.fillna` (`generic.py:6391`), `select_dtypes`/`_get_numeric_data`, `DataFrame.apply` (`frame.py:15751`), `unique_dtypes` in repr/info (`generic.py:7136`), and twice per `iloc` setitem (`indexing.py:944, 975`). For wide, fragmented managers each call is O(nblocks) Python iteration plus an object-array allocation.

### Numbers (1000-col DataFrame, 335 blocks, mixed f8/i8/object)

| call | current | with cache | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mgr.get_dtypes()` | 47 us | 0.08 us | **608x** |
| `df.dtypes` | 58 us | 8.7 us | **6.7x** |

Caching saves the full cost on cache hits; `df.dtypes` retains ~8 us of unavoidable Series-construction overhead.

### Proposed change

Add a `_dtypes_cache` attribute on the manager, populated lazily in `get_dtypes()` and invalidated alongside the existing `_blknos` / `_interleaved_dtype` cache hooks (`managers.py:1411, 1497` and other block-mutation sites). The same invalidation pattern is already in place — adding one more entry is mechanical.

### Caveats

- The cached array must not be mutated in place by callers. A quick audit of callers shows they only read it (equality checks, `.take`, iteration) — no in-place writes — but worth confirming during review.
- `SingleBlockManager` already has only one block; the cache is still cheap and consistent.

Happy to put up a PR.

title: DEPR: deprecate set_eng_float_format
body: Claude wrote this at my request. ## Proposal Deprecate `pd.set_eng_float_format()` in favor of using `pd.set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(...))` directly. Human Update Or just deprecate without an alternative. I haven't seen any evidence that anyone uses this. ## Rationale `set_eng_float_format` is a legacy convenience function (added in v0.5.0) that is a thin wrapper around `set_option`: ```python def set_eng_float_format(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=False): set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(accuracy, use_eng_prefix)) ``` It is the only top-level `pd.set_*` function that exists outside the options API, making it an odd outlier in the public API. This was already identified in #15610, where the consensus was to integrate this into the options machinery or deprecate it. **Evidence of minimal usage:** - **GitHub code search** yields ~30 results for `set_eng_float_format` outside pandas-dev/pandas. The vast majority are vendored copies of pandas, type stubs, or re-exports (xorbits, modin, Apache Beam, pyparallel, pandas-stubs, etc.). Only **2** results are actual user code calling this function. - **Stack Overflow** has **zero** questions or answers mentioning `set_eng_float_format`. - **Only 2 bug reports** have ever been filed against this function in the pandas issue tracker (#11981 in 2016, #15610 in 2017). The replacement is straightforward and equally concise: ```python # Before pd.set_eng_float_format(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=True) # After from pandas.io.formats.format import EngFormatter pd.set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=True)) ``` This keeps `EngFormatter` available (it is not being deprecated), removes a one-off top-level function that doesn't fit the options API pattern, and simplifies the public API surface. Closes #15610.

title: [TEST]: Plotting tests fail with matplotlib 3.11.0 — color cycle returns RGB tuples instead of hex strings
body:
## BUG: Plotting tests fail with matplotlib 3.11.0 — color cycle returns RGB tuples instead of hex strings

### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from pandas.plotting._matplotlib.style import get_standard_colors

print(f"matplotlib: {matplotlib.__version__}")  # 3.11.0
print(f"pandas: {pd.__version__}")              # 3.0.3

# Returns hex strings with mpl 3.10.x, RGB tuples with mpl 3.11.0
colors = get_standard_colors(num_colors=3)
print(colors)
# mpl 3.10.9: ['#1f77b4', '#ff7f0e', '#2ca02c']
# mpl 3.11.0: [(0.122..., 0.467..., 0.706...), (1.0, 0.498..., 0.055...), (0.173..., 0.627..., 0.173...)]

# Same issue with Line2D.get_color()
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2, 3])
print(repr(line.get_color()))
# mpl 3.10.9: '#1f77b4'
# mpl 3.11.0: (0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765)
plt.close()

# The colors are numerically identical:
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
print(to_hex((0.12156862745098039, 0.4666666666666667, 0.7058823529411765)))
# '#1f77b4'
```

### Issue Description

With matplotlib 3.11.0 (released 2026-06-12), the default property cycle now returns colors as RGB tuples rather than hex strings. This causes 5 pandas plotting tests to fail:

- `tests/plotting/test_boxplot_method.py::TestDataFramePlots::test_colors_in_theme[default-expected1]`
- `tests/plotting/test_series.py::TestSeriesPlots::test_pie_series_autopct_and_fontsize`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[1-expected_name0]`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[3-expected_name1]`
- `tests/plotting/test_style.py::TestGetStandardColors::test_default_colors_named_undefined_prop_cycle[12-expected_name2]`

The upstream matplotlib change is https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/pull/29469 ("Separate property cycle handling from _process_plot_var_args"), merged in commit [`ec65514`](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/commit/ec655143528f8e8dbc7897cc3c1e59865672c7ef) and released as part of [matplotlib 3.11.0](https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/releases/tag/v3.11.0). This refactored the internal property cycle machinery into a dedicated class. As a side effect, the default `axes.prop_cycle` rcParam now stores colors as `(R, G, B)` float tuples rather than hex strings.

The relevant matplotlib milestone: https://github.com/matplotlib/matplotlib/milestone/96

All affected APIs are public:
- `mpl.rcParams['axes.prop_cycle']` — iterating over the cycler now yields `{'color': (R, G, B)}` dicts instead of `{'color': '#rrggbb'}` dicts
- `Line2D.get_color()` — returns whatever format was stored in the cycle, now a tuple instead of a string

The behavior change is observable through these public APIs, though matplotlib has never formally guaranteed a specific color *format* (both hex strings and RGB tuples are valid matplotlib color specifications). The pandas tests assert a specific format (hex strings) rather than comparing semantically.

### Expected Behavior

Tests should pass with matplotlib 3.11.0. The test assertions should either:

1. Normalize colors before comparison (e.g., using `matplotlib.colors.to_hex()` or `matplotlib.colors.same_color()`), or

Additionally, if `get_standard_colors()` has a documented contract about its return format, it may be worth normalizing the output within that function itself so downstream consumers aren't affected by matplotlib's internal representation changes.

title: PERF: Avoid drop_duplicates(keep=False) in DataFrame.__getitem__ for single-column access
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

Observed (before fix): With n = 1000000 columns, 1000 accesses can take on the order of several seconds because each access builds a new Index via drop_duplicates(keep=False).

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/frame.py#L4162-L4169


```code
import pandas as pd
import timeit

# DataFrame with many columns and duplicate names; one column "key" appears once
n = 1000000
cols = ["a"] * (n - 1) + ["key"]
df = pd.DataFrame(0, index=range(10000), columns=cols)


# Repeated single-column access (e.g. in a loop or pipeline)
def access():
    for _ in range(100):
        _ = df["key"]


# Current state: each df["key"] calls columns.drop_duplicates(keep=False) → O(n) + allocation

sec = timeit.timeit(access, number=10)
print(f"1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): {sec:.2f}s")
```

Output

```
1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): 8.69s
```

Expected: Single-column access when the key appears once should not rebuild the Index on every access; runtime should be much lower (e.g. well under 1 second for 1000 accesses).

Suggested Fix

```
if not is_mi:
    try:
        loc = self.columns.get_loc(key)
        if isinstance(loc, int):
            return self._get_item(key)
    except (KeyError, InvalidIndexError):
        pass
elif is_mi and self.columns.is_unique and key in self.columns:
    return self._getitem_multilevel(key)
```

Output would be

```
1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): 0.04s
```

title: ENH: Add `df.corrupt()` accessor to inject random faults and typos for Data Science education
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

In Data Science and AI education, teaching students how to clean and preprocess "dirty data" (handling missing values, detecting outliers, removing duplicates, and fixing text typos) is a critical skill. 

Currently, professors and students struggle to find realistic, messy datasets for practice. When using clean benchmark datasets (like Iris or Titanic), users have to write long, repetitive custom scripts from scratch just to artificially mess up the data for testing and educational purposes. There is no built-in, one-stop tool in Pandas to inject controlled chaos into a DataFrame.


### Feature Description

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import random
import string

@pd.api.extensions.register_dataframe_accessor("corrupt")
class CorruptAccessor:
    """
    A vectorized Pandas DataFrame accessor to inject synthetic anomalies, 
    missing values, outliers, duplicates, and smart human-like typos 
    for educational and pipeline testing purposes.
    """
    def __init__(self, pandas_obj):
        self._obj = pandas_obj

    def _resolve_count(self, param, total_elements):
        """Helper to support both exact integer counts and float percentages."""
        if isinstance(param, float) and 0.0 <= param <= 1.0:
            return int(param * total_elements)
        elif isinstance(param, (int, np.integer)):
            return int(param)
        else:
            raise TypeError("Parameters must be either an int (count) or a float between 0.0 and 1.0 (ratio).")

    def __call__(self, num_nan=0, num_outliers=0, num_duplicates=0, num_typos=0, random_state=None):
        if random_state is not None:
            np.random.seed(random_state)
            random.seed(random_state)

        # Work on a deep copy to guarantee immutability of the source dataset
        df = self._obj.copy()
        num_rows, num_cols = df.shape
        total_cells = num_rows * num_cols
        
        if num_rows == 0 or num_cols == 0:
            return df

        # --- 1. Resolve and Validate Injection Targets ---
        n_nan = self._resolve_count(num_nan, total_cells)
        if n_nan > total_cells:
            raise ValueError(f"Resolved NaNs ({n_nan}) cannot exceed total cells ({total_cells}).")

        numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns
        total_numeric_cells = num_rows * len(numeric_cols)
        n_outliers = self._resolve_count(num_outliers, total_numeric_cells)
        if n_outliers > total_numeric_cells:
            raise ValueError(f"Resolved outliers ({n_outliers}) cannot exceed total numeric cells ({total_numeric_cells}).")

        n_duplicates = self._resolve_count(num_duplicates, num_rows)
        
        text_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'string']).columns
        total_text_cells = num_rows * len(text_cols)
        n_typos = self._resolve_count(num_typos, total_text_cells)
        if n_typos > total_text_cells:
            raise ValueError(f"Resolved typos ({n_typos}) cannot exceed total text cells ({total_text_cells}).")

        # --- 2. Vectorized Fault Injection Pipelines ---

        # Pipeline A: Global Vectorized NaN Injection
        if n_nan > 0:
            flat_indices = np.random.choice(total_cells, size=n_nan, replace=False)
            nan_mask = np.zeros(total_cells, dtype=bool)
            nan_mask[flat_indices] = True
            nan_mask = nan_mask.reshape(num_rows, num_cols)
            
            for i, col in enumerate(df.columns):
                col_mask = nan_mask[:, i]
                if col_mask.any():
                    df.iloc[col_mask, i] = np.nan

        # Pipeline B: Statistically Robust Outlier Injection (Vectorized per Column)
        if n_outliers > 0 and len(numeric_cols) > 0:
            flat_num_indices = np.random.choice(total_numeric_cells, size=n_outliers, replace=False)
            outlier_mask = np.zeros(total_numeric_cells, dtype=bool).reshape(num_rows, len(numeric_cols))
            outlier_mask.ravel()[flat_num_indices] = True
            
            for i, col in enumerate(numeric_cols):
                col_mask = outlier_mask[:, i]
                if col_mask.any():
                    std_dev = df[col].std()
                    if pd.isna(std_dev) or std_dev == 0:
                        std_dev = 1.0
                    df.loc[col_mask, col] = (df.loc[col_mask, col] * 3) + (5 * std_dev)

        # Pipeline C: Vectorized Duplicate Injection
        if n_duplicates > 0:
            duplicated_rows = df.sample(n=n_duplicates, replace=True, random_state=random_state)
            df = pd.concat([df, duplicated_rows], ignore_index=True)

        # Pipeline D: Smart Realistic Text Typo Injection
        if n_typos > 0 and len(text_cols) > 0:
            flat_text_indices = np.random.choice(total_text_cells, size=n_typos, replace=False)
            typo_mask = np.zeros(total_text_cells, dtype=bool).reshape(num_rows, len(text_cols))
            typo_mask.ravel()[flat_text_indices] = True
            
            def _mutate_string(val):
                """Helper to simulate realistic human typing errors dynamically."""
                s = str(val)
                if not s or s == "nan":
                    return s
                
                # Randomly pick an error type: deletion, substitution, or insertion
                operation = random.choice(['delete', 'substitute', 'insert'])
                random_char = random.choice(string.ascii_lowercase)
                
                if len(s) <= 1:
                    return s + random_char
                
                if operation == 'delete':
                    return s[:-1]
                elif operation == 'substitute':
                    return s[:-1] + random_char
                else:  # insert
                    return s + random_char

            for i, col in enumerate(text_cols):
                col_mask = typo_mask[:, i]
                if col_mask.any():
                    # Apply the dynamic typo mutation function strictly to the masked cells
                    df.loc[col_mask, col] = df.loc[col_mask, col].apply(_mutate_string)

        return df



### Alternative Solutions

### Current Workaround / Alternative Code:

Currently, users and educators have to write verbose, loop-heavy, or non-vectorized custom functions to perturb their data cell-by-cell. A typical suboptimal workaround looks like this:

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import random

def manual_corrupt(df, num_nan=0, num_typos=0):
    df_dirty = df.copy()
    
    # 1. Non-vectorized manual loop for NaNs
    if num_nan > 0:
        for _ in range(num_nan):
            r = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[0] - 1)
            c = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[1] - 1)
            df_dirty.iat[r, c] = np.nan
            
    # 2. Slow cell-by-cell scalar string manipulation for typos
    text_cols = df_dirty.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'string']).columns
    if num_typos > 0 and len(text_cols) > 0:
        for _ in range(num_typos):
            r = random.randint(0, df_dirty.shape[0] - 1)
            col = random.choice(text_cols)
            current_val = str(df_dirty.at[r, col])
            # Naive typo injection (just drops the last character)
            if len(current_val) > 1:
                df_dirty.at[r, col] = current_val[:-1]
                
    return df_dirty


### Additional Context

This feature would significantly benefit the Data Science, Machine Learning, and AI educational ecosystem (such as university courses, bootcamps, and online interactive notebooks). 

Teaching "Data Cleaning" is notoriously hard without messy data, and creating realistic "dirty data" natively with one simple, reproducible function call (`df.corrupt(...)`) would seamlessly close the gap between pristine benchmark da

title: BUG: Regression when using `.str[...]` accessor on `ArrowExtensionArray`
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> x = pd.Series(["abc"])
>>> x.str[0]
0    a
dtype: str
>>> x_converted = x.convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="pyarrow")
>>> x_converted.str[0]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-4>", line 1, in <module>
    x_converted.str[0]
    ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^
  File "...\pandas\core\strings\accessor.py", line 254, in __getitem__
    result = self._data.array._str_getitem(key)
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'ArrowExtensionArray' object has no attribute '_str_getitem'. Did you mean: '_str_istitle'?
```

### Issue Description

When using `.convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="pyarrow")`, the underlying array of string types is an `ArrowExtensionArray`. Previously, this class inherited string methods from `ArrowStringArrayMixin` and `BaseStringArrayMethods`. However, in 3.0.0, that was changed to remove `BaseStringArrayMethods` (#62155).

Unfortunately, `BaseStringArrayMethods` does not have full parity with `ArrowStringArrayMixin`. I did a quick search of the other differences, and `_str_getitem` appears to be the only difference that causes this problem.

I think `ArrowStringArrayMixin` or `ArrowExtensionArray` should implement the `_str_getitem` method, though another solution would be to have `.convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="pyarrow")` to produce an `ArrayStringArray` instead of an `ArrowExtensionArray` for string columns. I'm not familiar enough with the details of these types to know why we would prefer the latter.

### Expected Behavior

`x.str[0]` works for any string-typed `x`

title: BUG: missing deprecation warning about epoch timestamps in the index in to_json()
body:
When we have a datetime64 column and writing to JSON, we get a warning about the default "epoch" `date_format` being deprecated. 
However, when the datetime64 data is in the index, we don't get the warning, while we also get epoch values:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [pd.Timestamp("2012-01-01"), pd.Timestamp("2012-01-02")]})
>>> df.to_json()
Pandas4Warning: The default 'epoch' date format is deprecated and will be removed in a future version, please use 'iso' date format instead.
'{"A":{"0":1,"1":2},"B":{"0":1325376000000,"1":1325462400000}}'

>>> df.set_index("B").to_json()    # <-- no warning
'{"A":{"1325376000000":1,"1325462400000":2}}'
```

Both cases work fine with `date_format="iso"`:

```python
>>> df.to_json(date_format="iso")
'{"A":{"0":1,"1":2},"B":{"0":"2012-01-01T00:00:00.000","1":"2012-01-02T00:00:00.000"}}'
>>> df.set_index("B").to_json(date_format="iso")
'{"A":{"2012-01-01T00:00:00.000":1,"2012-01-02T00:00:00.000":2}}'
```

But so if we want to be able to change to `"iso"` by default in 4.0 for both cases, we also have to warn now in both cases
